newsitem.title: USA: Clinton signs anti-terrorism bill into law.
newsitem.headline: Clinton signs anti-terrorism bill into law.

text.p: Surrounded by people who have lost loved ones in airline crashes, several of them crying, President Bill Clinton on Wednesday signed into law a bill that tightens airport security against terrorism.

Conceived after the July 17 crash of TWA Flight 800, which exploded over the Atlantic off Long Island and killed all 230 people aboard, the bill provides for using more sophisticated baggage-scanners and bomb-sniffing dogs at airports.
It also calls for hiring dozens of new Federal Bureau of Investigation agents to fight terrorism and seeks to improve assistance to the families of victims after air disasters.
"Because of these improvements, Americans will not only feel safer, they will be safer," Clinton said at a signing ceremony held in the Old Executive Office Building next door to the White House.

The White House invited the relatives of victims of several air crashes, including TWA Flight 800, to the event and some of the women who stood with Clinton as he signed the legislation broke down crying as they watched.

"America has the will, and we are finding the ways, to increase security against the terrorist threat on all fronts," he said. "We cannot make the world risk-free, but we can reduce the risks we face."

The measures, embedded in legislation funding the Federal Aviation Administration, followed a variety of other steps included in other bills to prevent attacks on federal facilities at home and diplomatic buildings abroad.
"We are ... stepping up our law enforcement efforts with more agents and prosecutors and we're sending a message to terrorists that they will pay the full price for their deeds," Clinton added.
There much was criticism after the TWA Flight 800 crash, whose cause has still not been determined, that the airline was slow to inform families of the deaths.

Partly as a result, the legislation signed Wednesday designated the National Transportation Safety Board, which investigates air crashes, as having primary responsibility for assisting families after such disasters.
It also requires airlines to keep more accurate and complete passenger manifests so that the identities of those involved in air crashes can be ascertained quickly.

The bill, which authorises $19 billion for the FAA over the next two years, also issues new rules for record-setting flights in an effort to prevent crashes like the one that killed seven-year-old pilot Jessica Dubroff last April.
Dubroff died in Wyoming when her plane crashed while she was trying to become the youngest pilot to fly across the country.
